[given_date] is when I learn I've made this forecast. I don't remember creating this forecast. I'm pretty sure I haven't already made a forecast of this specific event. I estimate a probability of 0.02 that the event will happen before the forecast deadline and of 0.43 between the forecast deadline and the first planned deadline. I use these estimates to get probabilities of 0.02, 0.19, 0.39, 0.57, and 0.82 for the five deadlines.คุณสามารถ
{"2026": 0.02, "2030": 0.19, "2035": 0.39, "2040": 0.57, "2050": 0.82}ᨪ))

Pace of mathematical progress is not linear and the state of the art varies greatly between different subfields. This forecast is heavily informed by my knowledge of a few problem areas such as machine learning. AI has not made a major contribution to mathematics in any area, particularly number theory, so it is conservative in assuming a low probability of solving one of the remaining unsolved problems. The problems at the forecast date are easy steps below the current frontier. A solution would be valuable, utilizing state-of-the-art problem-solving techniques. ItemType: ranked-choice-chief-editorial

Claim: I highly question the idea that a mathematical breakthrough, even a small one, happens often as a result of using AI. This is largely so because research in mathematics is less structured than research in other fields (for example CS or bioinformatics) and the current AI systems are still incapable of utilising their imagination. More concretely, the NDXI thing means nothing: the mathematical wisdom that such things contractors can acquire will only give them a slight march over mathematicians who don't use AI, and of course they are severely limited in what they can utilise for finding theorems and proofs. ItemType: argument

Claim: Turn your knowledge of machine learning on its head, then use that knowledge as if it were applied understanding in core areas of mathematics, rather than other fields covered by machine learning.
1. "Core" means actually used by practitioners in the field. The core numbers theory-paper is not math 94, but the elementary number theory course in college.
2. Machine learning methods have to be applied directly. Suppose you want to reconcile two proven statements of number theory. A neural net that can apply the central median of a set-wise approach and convert that into a type morphing of the direct focal number could partially work/give hints for introducing AH bijections for eliminating central discs. ItemType: argument

Claim: Anything relying on proof by contradiction has to be thrown out since COVID19.
* proof by contradiction is one of the few ways math has proven interesting theorems
* all math results include contradiction. ItemType: argument

Claim: A neural network with an optimization algorithm (gradient descent) is in fact a linear algebra li/. The optimal parameters lie on a convex closure of the parameter space, and there is a unique minimum. So there isn't anything more complicated to be done here by modern math.
* modern math is a problem of finding combinatorial structures/combinations/applications that are responsible for the global convergence of a weak function class to a local, linear approximation, and the one best structure that adds something new to an existing weak function class. ItemType: argument

Claim: At most half of the paper in every area/hierarchy is "research" of any value. The rest claim to have provided something new, but aren't really able to. Any new insight (either a new way in which something works, new design choices or a new core theorem) requires a structurally challenging program. It is humanly possible for the system to play a part in this process, but it is not possible for it to be a main contributor to it. ItemType: argument

# Interpretation

* We start off from zero passive knowledge of AI. This is true for almost all unsolved Millennium Prize Problems: there is no known use of machine learning early in their history.
* We infer one million relevant papers per area per year published, indexed, pre-processed by plausibly enough machines, and stored in roughly a petabyte of proper storage. See the Semantic Scholar backend. This number fits with, but does not require, a similar growth in academic interest and public valuation of the included papers.
* Roughly half of this is unimportant, low-quality mathematics from a human perspective. If we trust the author assessment, a quarter of this is good. The AI performs a literature review of all of these papers, focusing on those that will likely be trust-worthy, detailed, and tractable for its fellow AIs (i.e. similar style papers, or stylised numerical results) and attempts to build a logical model of current knowledge.
* Precisely half of the "good" papers are actually irrelevant - they are about non-quantitative matters of exposition and context. Through plausible and legitimate human experience, all mathematicians quickly gain a rough idea of what is important in a field.
* Of the remaining "good but relevant" papers, a quotient of this translates into a similar kind of paper itself, and the rest is new insight.
* Since papers have checkable results of a type called "small", but none of a type called "big", the AI can only ask for "small" as expected by real "good", "relevant" specialists of the field; otherwise it decides to look elsewhere in the corpus, assume they have found a real reason related to their specialized degree of cleverness, or take a risk and submit a paper to the council.
* To find a novel and useful big insight, they rephrase the problem again by combining multiple equivalence classes of the equivalence relation congruence modulo having the same kind of core value, cutting away the effect from evaluating the constant and differentiating the gradient in the function, looking for higher order values regarding the number of degrees of freedom and the different complexities of the bases, breaking apart the explicit order symmetry of the specific problem and then synthesizing it through a contraction, and generally lawfully adding rule sets together without adding the contradiction of identity and base case into the contractive protocol - continuing to do so until the algorithm stops working, leaving it to the specialists to talk about the pros and cons of deciding which as yet unknown difference that worked to decide a new specific value instance/interesting concave vs. crescent curve that the algorithm returns.
* The AI gives us its model, which concurs. Our model is quite different since it is based on intuition gained from our own experience. It predicts that knowledge has exploded exponentially and math does not fit that model. 
* Note that if they had predicted a continuous explosion of knowledge and math fits that model, we would have started our section on Evidence Suitability with a more deterrence-inducing interpretation. ItemType: interpretationmbH)
formatted_prompt:
<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

For each deadline, state your probability that this event will have occurred by then. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
